business_type_notes: Both GBP categories are A (Electrician Calibration Pack v1, section 2: Electrician is A plus emergency, Security System Supplier is A project), so category_types is empty. Urgent against planned is split by page, not by category: the library's emergency column (Emergency electrician, Electrical fault finding and repairs) switches the emergency variant on when the client confirms call outs; every other page gets the plain briefs. Inside the planned pages the pack's three way split is carried in the card briefs: obligation led (who the work is for, what date brings it, what the result is used for; never a symptom) for EICR and electrical testing, Landlord electrical certificates, PAT testing, Smoke and heat alarms, Fire alarm systems and Emergency lighting; problem led (symptom, cause in the circuit, consequence) for Sockets and switches, Consumer unit upgrades, Rewiring and Extractor fan installation; desire led (the customer's situation, never an invented symptom; the library's desire_led column) for EV charger installation, Lighting installation, Garden and outdoor lighting, Smart home installation, Home cinema and audio visual, Data and network cabling, Solar PV and battery storage, Cooker and hob installation, Electric shower installation, CCTV installation, Intruder alarms, Access control and door entry and Commercial electrical work. Rewiring stays problem led (the pack lists it there first; the renovation reading is a line in card 3). Obligation led takes schedule led's place and is written into the type A briefs, not a type of its own. None of the work is a recurring round, so there is no type B. Not a seasonal trade: seasonal_trade is off; the two real timings (outdoor circuits before paving and planting, a rewire before decorating) sit in the desire cards and the timing briefs.

steps.title: Tell Us What You Need
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to send first: what the job is (a report by a date, a new circuit, a fault, a charger), roughly how old the house is if they know, a photo of the fuse board from where they stand. No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set. Never an instruction to open a socket, a fitting or the fuse board.

steps.title: We Look at the Wiring and Price the Job
steps.brief: The visit and what gets looked at: the fuse board, the earthing and bonding, the circuits the job touches and the routes the cable would take, access under floors and in the loft (the Table A survey stages). Follows [CV: quote_method]; only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Testing on the visit only from confirmed practices. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps.title: We Book a Date and Do the Work
steps.brief: The start date is agreed in advance, to suit the customer. What the customer gets at the end: the work tested and the certificate for it, which the Table A rows end every job with; the building control side only where the client values confirm the business is registered to certify its own work. Never mention the price, the quote or changes to the plan (step 2 and Why choose us own them). Never restates the start time (FAQ 4 owns it).

step_2_no_visit.title: We Price Your Job
step_2_no_visit.brief: Say a price is agreed before any work starts. Describe how the price is reached only from [CV: quote_method]; when quote_method is blank, name no method at all (no photos, call, video or visit). Only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps_emergency.title: Call Us
steps_emergency.brief: What to say: what is happening, which rooms have lost power, whether anything smells hot or has scorch marks, whether the trip switch goes straight back off. What to do meanwhile, in plain words from the Table B emergency row and the pack's safe basics: turn that circuit off at the fuse box, or the main switch if they cannot tell which, unplug what was on it, keep away from anything scorched or wet. Nothing beyond that: never an instruction to open or touch a fitting or the board. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps_emergency.title: We Make It Safe
steps_emergency.brief: What usually happens on arrival: the fault assessed, the dangerous part switched off or otherwise made safe, the immediate fault found where it can be (the Table A emergency electrician stages). An arrival time only as the business gives it on the call; no window written here unless [CV: response_time] is set. The price for the call out agreed before anyone comes out only from the price_agreed_before_work practice and [CV: quote_method]; a call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: price_list]. Never restates 'free'. 'Same day' only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes; round the clock cover only when [CV: emergency_callouts] or [CV: out_of_hours_available] gives it.

steps_emergency.title: We Fix It, or Book the Repair
steps_emergency.brief: The fault repaired on the visit where it is found and the part is to hand; otherwise the house left safe with that circuit off and the rest back on, and a date agreed for the fault finding and the permanent repair (Table A: a call out may finish with the wiring made safe rather than fully repaired; Table E: an emergency visit and a full diagnosis can be separate work). The customer told plainly what is off and why (Table B: a circuit left off without a clear handover gets switched back on). Never promise a same visit fix. Never mention the price.

the price growing once the floorboards are up and the plaster is off

work they cannot judge once the walls are made good, and no paperwork to show it was tested

faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: complaints_process] only.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your work?

A maker's warranty on a charger, an alarm or a fitting only from [CV: manufacturer_warranty]; a scheme's work guarantee (Table D: some schemes offer a conditional one) only from the client values, described, never promised.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after the job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Used when nothing in cover_chain other than insurance is confirmed. Open with what the customer does: tell us what isn't right and we'll look at it. No promise to come back or put it right for free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: How soon can you start?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: start_time] only, as given. Code adds "bigger projects are booked further ahead" only when that practice is confirmed. Urgent faults handled differently only when [CV: same_day_available] or [CV: emergency_callouts] says so.

faq_slots.question: Is the quote free and no obligation?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [QUOTE_FREE] and [CV: quote_method]. A fault finding visit is work, not a quote: say so only where the client values separate the two.

faq_slots.question: How do your quotes work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] only.

faq_slots.question: How long does electrical work take?
faq_slots.answer_brief: No standard duration exists (Table G): give what decides it, in plain words, from the Table A timing cells and the Table F rows: how many circuits, how far the cable has to travel and through what, whether rooms are lived in while the work goes on, and the making good afterwards. A figure only from [CV: typical_jobs]. Say which jobs need the power off for a spell (a board change: the Table A consumer unit timing cell) without a length of time.

faq_slots.question: Why does my trip switch keep going off?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Say first that the switch going off is the protection working. Then three genuinely different causes in plain words, from the Table B fault finding row and the pack's cause in the circuit: an appliance that is leaking current to earth, water that has got into a garden socket or an outside light, a screw driven into a cable or a connection that has worked loose and is heating. Then what the local housing adds, then the fix: the circuit tested piece by piece to find it (Table A fault finding). Never tell the reader to hold the switch on or to change the device; never a step that opens the board.

faq_slots.question: Do I need a new fuse box?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Honest first: an older board is not dangerous by its age alone (Table E metal consumer units and rewire scope rows). Then what a newer board adds, in plain words from the Table C RCD row with "usually": protection that cuts the power the instant current leaks where it should not, which old rewireable fuses do not give. Then that a change begins by testing each circuit first, since a new board may reveal faults the old fuses let pass (Table A consumer unit stages, Table E what a change includes). Never a fire statistic, never a test as a route to a sale, never a regulation's name or year.

faq_slots.question: How often should a house have its wiring tested?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Organised by who the home belongs to, from the Table E rows: a rented home on the interval the landlord rules give, or sooner where the last report says so; an owner's home on the interval the owner occupier row recommends, as advice rather than law; a sale, a new tenancy or a change of use as common points to test. The intervals only as the rows state them, never a regulation name. What the report is (a condition report with an overall outcome, not a pass certificate: Table E outcome row). Nothing about this business doing the test unless the services list has the page.

faq_slots.question: Does my electrical work need building control sign off?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the Table C building control notification rows and the Table E notification rows and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": a new circuit, a new fuse board, or work close to a bath or shower is usually notifiable; a like for like swap or an extra socket on an existing circuit elsewhere usually is not, though it is still tested and certificated. Then the routes: an electrician registered with a scheme certifies their own work and the paperwork follows; otherwise building control is told before the work starts. Which route this business uses only from [CV: materials_methods] (registered to certify its own work) or the client values. Never a regulation's name or number, never a measurement, never scheme membership as this business's practice unless confirmed.

Paperwork: registered to certify our own work (competent person scheme)
Other: old boards and cable taken away

cards.title: A trip switch that keeps going off
cards.brief: Problem led: the power goes and the switch at the fuse box is down again, once a week or every time the kettle goes on. Say first that the switch going off is the protection doing what it is for. The one cause this card makes: current leaking to earth from one appliance, one fitting or one damaged cable on that circuit (the Table B fault finding row, the pack's cause in the circuit). Say what finding it involves in plain words: the circuit tested piece by piece until the leak shows (Table A fault finding: establish the symptoms and the circuit, inspect and test to locate, repair, retest). What the customer can safely do: leave the switch off and unplug what was on that circuit; never hold it on, never change the device, never open the board. On a Security System Supplier page the card reads as an alarm that goes off for no reason or a camera that keeps dropping out, with the cause in the sensor's position or the set up (Table B intruder alarms and CCTV). Never a fire statistic.
cards.mechanism: current leaking to earth from one appliance, fitting or cable

cards.title: A report or certificate you need by a date
cards.brief: Obligation led, never a symptom: a landlord with a let coming up for its inspection, a seller whose buyer's solicitor has asked for a report, a business whose insurer wants the alarm and the emergency lights tested with the records to show. The one cause this card makes: a date set by a tenancy, a sale or an insurer, not by the state of the wiring. Say who the test is for and what the result is used for, from the Table C and Table E rows only: the landlord's interval and the time allowed to put faults right as the rows give them, the copies that go to the tenant, the owner's interval as advice; an EICR comes back satisfactory or unsatisfactory and what each code means only as the Table C codes row states it. Then the practical point: a test booked well ahead of the date leaves room for anything it finds. On a Security System Supplier page: the standard a monitoring company or an insurer asks for, from the Table C intruder alarm and Table D rows only; otherwise the card reads as the Electrician's. Never a regulation's name, edition or number; never a test written as the first step to a sale.
cards.mechanism: a date set by a tenancy, a sale or an insurer, not by the wiring

cards.title: Scorch marks or a hot smell at a socket or switch
cards.brief: Problem led: a socket warm to the hand, brown marks round a faceplate, a crackle when a switch is used, a plug that sits loose (the Table B sockets and switches row). The one cause this card makes: a connection that has worked loose, so the current heats it every time the circuit is used. Say why it matters without alarm: the heat builds while it is in use, so the sensible step is to turn that circuit off at the fuse box and stop using the socket until it has been opened and tested; nothing beyond that for the reader to do (the pack's safe basics). What the fix usually involves from Table A: the circuit made safe, the connection or the fitting replaced, the circuit tested before it goes back on. On a Security System Supplier page the card reads as the wired side of a system: a power supply or a connection that has worked loose, so a camera drops offline or a door release fails (Table B access control, CCTV). Never 'death trap', never a fire statistic.
cards.mechanism: a connection that has worked loose and heats in use

cards.title: Adding something the house was never wired for
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: an electric car on the drive, a gas hob going and an induction one coming in, an electric shower, power to a garden office or a workshop, a loft room with no sockets. The one cause this card makes: a new load or a new circuit asked of a supply, a fuse board and an earth sized for the house as it was. What decides it, from the Table A survey stages and the Table E bonding row: how much the supply has in hand, whether the board has room for another circuit, whether the earthing and bonding are sound before anything is added, and the route the cable takes. What the work gives them in plain words: a circuit of its own with its own protection, tested and certificated. For a charger the network operator is told as the Table C row has it, said without the acronym where the copy can. On a Security System Supplier page the card is the situation that leads to cameras or an alarm: a side gate nobody can see from the kitchen, a drive that delivery vans use, a shop door after closing (Table A CCTV: the views and the positions surveyed first). Never a symptom invented for it, never a charging speed, a grant or a saving unless the client values give it.
cards.mechanism: a new load on a supply and a board sized for the old house

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] in [CITY]

cards.title: How many circuits are involved
cards.brief: More circuits, more sockets, more fittings, more detectors or more cameras move the price more than anything else (the Table F rows for rewiring, consumer units, testing, alarms and CCTV). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Getting the cable where it needs to go
cards.brief: A route chased into the wall and plastered over against one run on the surface, floors up and lofts crawled, rooms that are lived in while the work goes on, a trench across the garden (Table F: concealed routes needing opening and making good, occupied rooms, trenching and reinstatement). Say why a hidden route costs more time; name a method only from [CV: materials_methods].

cards.title: What the testing turns up
cards.brief: Faults already on the circuits, earthing or bonding that has to be brought up to standard before the new work can be certificated, a board whose circuits nobody can identify (Table F consumer units, sockets and shower rows; Table E: changing a board can expose faults already there). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only, and that what a test finds is priced as it is found, never as a surprise on the invoice; the extra_work_agreed_first practice only when confirmed.

cards.title: The fittings and protection you choose
cards.brief: A board with a device on every circuit against a shared one, surge protection, a tethered charger against a socket, LED downlights against surface fittings, a monitored alarm against a bell on the wall (the Table A materials cells). Name an option only if the trade facts or [CV: materials_methods] give it. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

faq_slots.question: How much does [WORK_LOWER] cost in [CITY]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Prices only from [CV: price_list]; otherwise the three things that move the price for this kind of work (the number of circuits, the cable route, what the testing finds) and how the quote is given, from [CV: quote_method] only. A call out charge only from price_list.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your [WORK_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Start with yes, then the terms from [CV: guarantee_years] and [CV: guarantee_scope]. A maker's warranty on a charger, a board or an alarm only from [CV: manufacturer_warranty]. Described, never promised.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured for [WORK_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, with a plausible electrical example that does not suggest carelessness. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after the job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to (Table C). No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What [WORK_LOWER] do you take on?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The jobs themselves, named from the card list (the fault finding, the board changes, the rewires, the reports, the new circuits), and the size of job taken on, from the services list and [CV: typical_jobs] only. Link one service page. Never 'on this page', 'listed above' or 'the card list' as words: the reader sees no list, so name the work. Commercial or landlord work only where the services list has it.

faq_slots.question: What happens when I ask for a quote?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends, what the business looks at (the fuse board, the earthing, the routes: the Table A survey stages), what comes back. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set. Never testing on the visit as this business's practice unless confirmed.

faq_slots.question: Will the power be off while you work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the Table A timing cells only: a fuse board change needs the power off for the job, arranged in advance; an electric shower needs the water and the power off while it is connected; a new circuit or a repair usually means only that circuit off while it is worked on; a condition report needs each circuit reachable and the interruptions agreed first. No length of time (Table G: none is established). Nothing about when the job can start unless [CV: start_time] is set.

faq_symptom.frame: [SYMPTOM]: why does it happen, and what can be done?
faq_symptom.answer_brief: The symptom and its linked local issue, answered as asked. Put the cause in the circuit, in plain words (a connection heating, current leaking to earth, water in a fitting, a cable damaged, protection the house was built without), from the Table B rows. Then what the local housing adds, said as what homes of that era were built with and may still have, never that they are dangerous (Table E: age alone does not decide a rewire). Then what the business does about it: test to find it, then repair (Table A). What the reader can safely do stops at switching off and unplugging. One figure at most, and only one the facts rows state.

cards.title: A burning smell or scorch marks you can't place
cards.brief: A hot plastic smell with nothing cooking, brown marks spreading round a socket or a switch, a crackle or a spark when something is plugged in, smoke from the fuse board (the Table B emergency row). The one cause this card makes: a connection overheating out of sight, which gets hotter the longer the circuit stays on. What the customer does first, from the pack's safe basics: turn that circuit off at the fuse box, or the main switch if they cannot tell which, unplug what was on it, touch nothing that is scorched, then call. Why it cannot wait: the heat keeps building for as long as the circuit is used. What usually happens when they call, from the Table A emergency stages: the fault assessed, the dangerous part switched off or made safe, the immediate cause found where it can be, the circuit tested before it goes back on. Never an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set; round the clock cover only when [CV: emergency_callouts] gives it; never a fire statistic; nothing about smart homes or new work on this card.
cards.mechanism: a connection overheating out of sight

cards.title: A trip switch that won't stay on
cards.brief: The power goes, the switch at the fuse box is pushed back up and drops straight down again, or holds for a minute and goes (Table B emergency: sudden loss of power with a tripping breaker). The one cause this card makes: a fault still live on that circuit, which the switch is refusing to feed. What the customer does first: leave it off, unplug everything on that circuit, and if it then holds the fault is in something that was plugged in; if it still will not hold, the fault is in the wiring and the circuit stays off. Never hold it on, never swap the device, never open the board (Table B: putting the power back before the hazard is found puts the hazard back). What usually happens: the circuit tested to find the fault, repaired where it can be, or left off safely with the rest of the house back on and a date for the repair (Table A). Never promise the power back that visit.
cards.mechanism: a fault still live on the circuit the switch is refusing to feed

cards.title: Water where the electrics are
cards.brief: A leak from the bathroom coming through a ceiling light, rain inside an outside light, a flooded garden socket, a splash into a switch (Table B garden lighting: water visible inside a fitting, an outdoor light that trips again and again). The one cause this card makes: water bridging live parts inside a fitting. What the customer does first: turn that circuit off at the fuse box, touch neither the fitting nor its switch while anything is wet, keep the room's lights off until it has been looked at. Why it cannot wait: a wet fitting stays dangerous until it has been dried, opened and tested, and a trip switch that has not gone does not mean it is safe. What usually happens: made safe, the fitting opened and tested once dry, replaced where water has got into it, the route resealed outdoors (Table A fault finding: repair or replace the defective part; Table B: poor sealing admits water). Never a step that opens the fitting for the reader.
cards.mechanism: water bridging live parts inside a fitting

cards.title: Power gone in part of the house
cards.brief: The lights downstairs are fine and the kitchen sockets are dead, or one floor is dark and nothing at the fuse box looks any different. The one cause this card makes: one circuit lost to a fault, a connection that has failed or a blown fuse on an older board, while the rest carry on. What the customer does first: look whether the lights next door are off too, which points away from the house's own wiring; look at the fuse box without opening it, note which switch is down, and leave it down; unplug what was on that circuit. What usually happens when they call: the affected circuit found and tested (Table A: establish the symptoms and the circuit), the fault repaired on the visit where the part is to hand, or that circuit left off safely with the rest restored and a date agreed (Table A: a call out may end with the wiring made safe rather than fully repaired; Table E emergency versus fault find). Never promise the power back that visit; never a fridge or a freezer promise.
cards.mechanism: one circuit lost while the rest carry on

cards.title: Reaching the wiring
cards.brief: A socket or a board you can get straight to against cable under a floor or behind a finished wall (Table F: inaccessible wiring). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: A socket or switch that's hot to the touch
cards.brief: A faceplate warm under the hand, a plug that comes out brown, a crackle when the switch goes on, a smell of hot plastic nobody can place (the Table B sockets and switches and emergency rows). The one cause this card makes: a loose terminal arcing under load, which burns a little more each time the circuit is used. What the customer does first: turn that circuit off at the fuse box, unplug whatever was in it, touch nothing scorched, then call. Why it cannot wait: the damage grows while the power is on (Table B: continued use of the faulty circuit can cause shock or fire, said once and plainly). What usually happens on the visit: made safe, the connection or the fitting replaced, the circuit tested before it goes back on (Table A fault finding). Leads on the fault finding page; Emergency electrician reads it as the fuse board itself warm or smelling. Never an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set; never a fire statistic.
cards.mechanism: a loose terminal arcing under load

cards.title: A fuse board that trips again as soon as it's reset
cards.brief: The main switch or one trip drops the moment it is pushed up, or every time one thing is switched on (Table B: sudden loss of power with a tripping breaker). The one cause this card makes: the protection doing exactly what it is for, refusing to feed a fault it has found. What the customer does first: leave the switch down, unplug everything on that circuit, try it once more; if it holds, the fault was in something plugged in and that thing stays unplugged; if it drops again, the circuit stays off and they call. Never hold it on, never change the device for a bigger one, never open the board (Table B: restoring supply before the hazard is identified puts the hazard back). What usually happens: the circuit tested to find the fault, repaired where it can be, otherwise left off with the rest of the house running and a date for the repair (Table A). Leads on both urgent pages. Never promise the power back that visit.
cards.mechanism: the protection refusing to feed a fault it has found

cards.title: A light fitting or outside socket that's got wet
cards.brief: Water dripping from a ceiling rose after a bath overflowed, rain inside a porch light, a garden socket under a puddle, a fitting that trips every time it rains (the Table B garden lighting row: water visible inside the fitting, an outdoor light that keeps tripping). The one cause this card makes: moisture tracking across the terminals, which a trip switch may or may not catch. What the customer does first: turn that circuit off at the fuse box, leave the fitting and its switch alone while anything is wet, and keep the room's lights off until it has been looked at. Why it cannot wait: the fitting stays dangerous until it has dried, been opened and tested. What usually happens: made safe, the fitting opened and tested once dry, replaced where water has got in, the seal or the route put right outdoors so it does not happen again (Table A; Table B done badly: poor sealing admits water). Leads on both urgent pages. Never a step that opens the fitting for the reader.
cards.mechanism: moisture tracking across the terminals

faq_slots.question: Is this an emergency, or can it wait?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What counts as urgent for this service, from the card list and the Table B emergency row: a burning smell, scorching, sparks or smoke, a trip that will not stay on, water in a fitting, power lost to part of the house. What usually waits for a planned visit, from the Table B rows: a single light that flickers, a dead socket with nothing hot about it, a report that is due. Link the planned sibling page or the category page. Planned work is never dressed up as urgent.

problems.h2: What We Get Called to Most in [TOWN]

cards.title: Homes wired for a different decade
cards.brief: Rewireable fuses in the hall cupboard, two pin sockets behind the wardrobe, one socket a room with an extension lead doing the rest. The one cause this card makes: wiring and boards put in when the houses were built and added to in pieces ever since; the town profile dates the housing. Say what homes of that era were built with and what they may still have (the pack's anchor: cable with a rubber or a lead sheath and rewireable fuses in the older stock, estates wired once and extended since), never that they have it or that they are dangerous or overdue a rewire (Table E: age alone does not decide it). Tie the era to the work: testing before anything is added (Table E bonding row), a board change that starts with every circuit tested (Table A). Not a hot socket, not a tripping switch: the town's category and service pages own those.
cards.mechanism: wiring and boards put in with the houses and added to in pieces since

cards.title: Lets, shared houses and the inspection cycle
cards.brief: A landlord with several houses in the same streets, a letting agent with a list of dates, a shared student house with a licence to renew. The one cause this card makes: a tenancy calendar that sets the test dates, not the state of the wiring; the town profile gives the share of rented and shared homes. What it means for the work: condition reports on the interval the Table C landlord row gives, the time allowed to put faults right, the copies to tenants, all only as the rows state them; a licence condition only as the dossier gives it (Table G: licence conditions vary by council, never a national checklist). Never that the town's landlords are behind, never a regulation's name. Not the report itself: the testing pages own what it checks.
cards.mechanism: a tenancy calendar that sets the test dates

cards.title: Terraces with nowhere to park a charger
cards.brief: An electric car and a front door that opens onto the pavement, a cable across the path, a charger wanted where the only parking is on the street. The one cause this card makes: the gap between the house's supply and where the car actually stands; the town profile gives the street pattern (terraces on street parking, estates with drives). What it means for the work: a drive makes a charger straightforward (Table A EV: supply assessed, the network operator told, the earthing designed), while a charger across a public pavement is not covered by the home permission (Table C permitted development row) and depends on whatever the council allows, said only as the dossier gives it; never a council rule invented. Not the earthing itself: the next card and the EV page own that.
cards.mechanism: the gap between the house's supply and where the car stands

cards.title: Supplies that come in on poles
cards.brief: A farmhouse, a cottage at the end of a lane, a row of houses fed from a pole in the field: the town profile says where the supply arrives overhead. The one cause this card makes: a supply that arrives on poles and takes its earth at the house rather than from the network's cable (the pack's anchor). What it means for the work: the earthing tested, and sometimes improved, before a charger, an outdoor circuit or a new board goes in (Table C EV earthing row, Table E bonding row), said in plain words without the terms. Where the town has no rural fringe the card reads as its conservation areas and listed homes instead: a charger, a camera or a light on the front of a listed house needs more thought and sometimes consent (Table C listed building row, 'usually', never the Act's name). Never a judgement on the supply's safety.
cards.mechanism: a supply that arrives on poles and earths at the house

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] in [TOWN]

cards.title: Getting cable through an older house
cards.brief: Solid walls that have to be chased and made good, floors that come up in short boards, lofts with no boards at all, plaster that cannot be cut in a listed house (Table F rewiring: concealed routes, making good, protected fabric). Say why that adds time; the town profile says which streets are which. No figure.

cards.title: Flats, shared houses and tenants' diaries
cards.brief: Access arranged round several tenants, a report that needs every circuit reachable and the interruptions agreed first, work in rooms that are lived in (Table F landlord certificates: difficult tenant access; Table A EICR timing cell). Say it plainly, from the profile where it gives the tenure. No figure.

cards.title: The supply the street was given
cards.brief: An older street's supply with less in hand for a charger, a shower or a battery, a long cable run to the board, the network operator's process where the supply has to be looked at first (Table F EV and solar rows: supply upgrade, long run, the application). Said as what the work meets, never as a judgement on the street. No figure.

cards.title: Conservation areas and listed homes
cards.brief: Where the town has conservation areas or listed buildings, a charger, a panel, a camera or a light on a front wall and a new cable route through old plaster can need consent, and some things cannot be done at all (Table C listed building and permitted development rows, 'usually', never the Act's or the area's official name). From the dossier rules only; otherwise consent as something that sometimes applies. No figure.

faq_slots.question: How much does [WORK_LOWER] cost in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Prices only from [CV: price_list]; otherwise the things that push the price up in a town like this (the age of the house and its cable routes, access in a let, the supply) and how the quote is given, from [CV: quote_method] only.

faq_slots.question: How soon can you get to [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: start_time] and [CV: response_time] only. The town is in the area covered; nothing about distance unless [CV: travel_distance] is set. Urgent faults handled differently only when [CV: same_day_available] or [CV: emergency_callouts] says so.

faq_slots.question: Do you cover [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes: the town and the villages around it (code lists them; name none). How the business reaches it from its base only from the client values. Link one page in this town.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your work in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Start with yes, then the terms from [CV: guarantee_years] and [CV: guarantee_scope]. Described, never promised.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after the job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What happens when I ask for a quote in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends, what the business looks at (the fuse board, the earthing, the routes), what comes back. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: Will the power be off while you work in my home?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the Table A timing cells only: a fuse board change needs the power off for the job, arranged in advance; a new circuit or a repair usually means only that circuit off while it is worked on; a condition report needs the circuits reachable and the interruptions agreed first. Where the town profile gives the housing (flats on a shared supply, lets), say what it does to the arrangements. No length of time. Nothing about when the job can start unless [CV: start_time] is set.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How many circuits and boards
cards.brief: A small house on one board against more circuits or a second distribution board (Table F EICR). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: What the report finds
cards.brief: The report records what it finds and rates the installation satisfactory or unsatisfactory; it is not a pass certificate (Table E). What the codes mean only as Table E has them, in plain words. Remedial work and any further investigation are priced after the report, as their own job, never inside it (Table F: necessary fault investigation). The report is not a fault find (Table B). Extra work agreed before it is done only from the extra_work_agreed_first practice.

cards.title: Getting to the board and the accessories
cards.brief: Equipment that can be reached against a board behind stored things or accessories behind furniture, an occupied home where the power going off has to be agreed (Table F: inaccessible equipment; Table A timing cell). Say why each adds time and give no figure.

cards.title: The records and the paperwork
cards.brief: A clear circuit schedule and the last report to hand against limited records and circuits that have to be identified first (Table F). The report itself comes with the visit, an EICR and not an installation certificate (Table A). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How many circuits in the property
cards.brief: A small flat against a larger let with more circuits (Table F landlord electrical certificates). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: What the report finds
cards.brief: The report is an EICR, satisfactory or unsatisfactory, not a pass certificate (Table E). A finding that needs remedial work or investigation is priced after the report, as its own job, never inside it (Table F: required investigation or remedial work). The deadlines for that work only from Table C and Table E, as the landlord's duty, never a threat. Extra work agreed before it is done only from the extra_work_agreed_first practice.

cards.title: Getting in to an occupied let
cards.brief: An empty flat against a let with a tenant whose visit has to be arranged, and a board and accessories that can be reached against ones that cannot (Table F: difficult tenant access). Say why it adds time and give no figure. Who arranges access is the landlord (Table C).

cards.title: The certificate and the paperwork
cards.brief: The last report to hand against missing documents (Table F). What the landlord gets: the report and, after remedial work, the certificate for that work and the written confirmation it was done (Table A landlord row). Who has to receive copies only from Table C. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How many items
cards.brief: A handful of appliances against a building full of them, and a list that exists against one that has to be made (Table F PAT testing: more items, incomplete inventory). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: What the test finds
cards.brief: A cracked plug, a frayed flex or a damaged casing is recorded (Table B). Any repair or replacement is priced after the test, as its own job, never inside it (Table F: damaged items needing follow up). Extra work agreed before it is done only from the extra_work_agreed_first practice.

cards.title: Items spread across a building
cards.brief: Everything in one room against items spread across floors or sites, and equipment that is hard to reach (Table F: dispersed equipment, difficult access). Say why it adds time and give no figure.

cards.title: The register and the paperwork
cards.brief: What the visit leaves behind: an equipment register and a test record (Table A). How often items are tested goes by the risk and the equipment, never that the law asks for every item each year (Table E PAT legal status). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Tell Us What You Need
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to send first: what kind of premises, roughly how many appliances and where they are, any list from a last test, and any date a licence or a policy asks for (Table G: those conditions vary, so check the particular one). No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Count the Appliances and Price the Visit
steps.brief: How the items are counted and the price reached, from [CV: quote_method] only: a list they already have, or a walk round where the site_visit_before_quote practice says so. What moves it (Table F: more items, dispersed equipment). Only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps.title: We Book a Date and Do the Work
steps.brief: The date is agreed in advance, to suit the customer. What usually happens, from the Table A PAT testing row: the equipment listed, each item inspected, the right test chosen for it, the results recorded and anything faulty pointed out. What the customer gets at the end: the equipment record. Never mention the price, the quote or changes to the plan. Never restates the start time (FAQ 4 owns it).
